newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Tax worry pushes Fiat to record low.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Tax worry pushes Fiat to record low.

text.p: The shares of Italian carmaker Fiat hit a near three-year low on Monday amid a lack of consumer confidence in its important domestic market and worries about the impact on exports from the high value of the lira.

The Italian car market hit the bottom in 1993 along with other European automotive markets, but while others nations recovered the Italian market has struggled and looks as if it could slip this year even below the levels seen three years ago.

Rocky consumer confidence in Italy has been further unsettled by worries over a new Eurotax, part of Italy's tough 1997 financial budget package aimed at pushing the nation towards its goal of joining a single European currency.
Fiat shares slipped below the key 4,000 lire level to close down 1.49 percent at 3,964 lire, their lowest level seen since early December 1993.
"The shares are oversold, but there is not that much short term buoyance," said car industry analyst Philip Ayton at brokers BZW in London.

Added uncertainty comes with Italy's 1997 budget, which aims to cut the national deficit by 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion). It includes tax increases such as the new Eurotax which, although unspecified as yet, is set to raise 12 trillion lire and is expected to target middle income Italians.
Many analysts had expected the 1996 domestic car market to match 1995's level of 1.73 million units, but now many see the market dipping even below 1993's 1.69 million.

Nick Potter, analyst at Credito Italiano, is now looking for an Italian car market of 1.6 to 1.65 million units in 1996. He said Fiat faced a very tough domestic market and probably higher than expected labour costs.
On the positive side, the situation is more encouraging than in 1993 when Fiat slipped to a record loss as the European car market collapsed, he added.

Fiat now has a renewed car range with the launch of its new medium-large Marea last month adding to earlier Punto and Bravo/Brava ranges. It is doing well in Europe outside Italy and the trading outlook is improving in its key Brazilian market.
Potter says the Italian stock market has increased four percent so far in 1996, but Fiat shares have fallen 25 percent and are likely to have touched bottom.

Last week's September Italian car figues were particularly poor for Fiat. In a whole market down 8.5 percent, Fiat registrated a 17.2 percent drop, with its market share tumbling to 41.16 percent from 46.72 percent in September 1995.
"Worries about extra taxes in the 1997 budget have added just one more negative to an already very depressed domestic car market," said one Milan-based industry analyst.
Fiat, like other industrial groups in Italy, also faces a dispute with engineering unions representing 1.5 million workers who are set to strike on November 15 to press demands for higher pay.

Plans to float at least 31 percent of Fiat's farm machinery division New Holland on the New York Stock Exchange later this year to raise up to $1.23 billion is seen at broadly neutral for Fiat's earnings this year.
Most analysts expect net profits to fall this year. Potter expects 1996 earnings of 1.8 trillion lire and BZW's Ayton 1.65 trillion, following 1.95 trillion in 1995 excluding extraordinaries.
Fiat reported a headline net profit of 2.15 trillion in 1995 in a continued recovery from its record loss of 1.78 trillion in 1993.
